summary: Describes how the Service Location Protocol can discover services in remote, non-local DNS domains. It defines DNS SRV records for SLP Directory Agents and discusses issues in combining SLP with DNS. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: Normally you can only ask neighbors where things are. This experimental idea uses the internet's phone book to find helpers in other neighborhoods.

subtitle: Using DNS SRV records to find SLP Directory Agents in other domains so services there can be discovered.

tldr.problem: SLP finds services in the local administrative domain, but its usual ways of learning about Directory Agents do not work for a remote domain.
tldr.mechanism: A DNS SRV record named _slpda lists a domain's Directory Agents. A User Agent queries it, picks one by priority and weight, and asks that agent for services in the default scope.
tldr.outcome: A user who already knows the remote domain name can discover services there. The RFC is Experimental, and RFC 8553 updates it.

today: RFC 3832 is an Experimental specification and is updated by RFC 8553. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Local and Remote Service Discovery
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (SLP, RFC 2608) lets User Agents (UAs) find services in the local administrative domain, either by multicasting to Service Agents or by asking a unicast Directory Agent (DA). To use a DA, a UA first has to learn about it through DHCP, static configuration or multicast. The last two are not generally applicable beyond the local administrative domain.

Remote service discovery means finding services in a given non-local DNS domain. DNS SRV (RFC 2782) supports that, but when several servers are found it can select only by priority and weight, not by properties like cost or quality. The RFC therefore proposes combining them: use DNS SRV to find a remote DA, then use SLP to query it.
sections.eli5: SLP is like asking the people on your street where the nearest printer is. This lets you look up the helper for a faraway street first, then ask that helper.

sections.title: The SRV Record for SLP Directory Agents
sections.content:
The record follows RFC 2782 and has the form _slpda._Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target. Here slpda is the symbolic service name, Proto is tcp or udp, and Target is the domain name of a DA.

To find DAs in example.com, a UA sends a DNS query for _slpda._tcp.example.com (or the _udp form), class IN, type SRV. The reply lists the remotely accessible DAs, for example two targets da1.example.com and da2.example.com on port 427 with priority 0 and weight 0.
sections.eli5: The phone book has a special entry type that says "the helpers for this neighborhood are over here".

sections.title: Domain, Scope and Applicability Rules
sections.content:
The remote domain must be known in advance, for instance by configuration or because the user types it in. There is no implied search order: for foo.bar.example.com a UA SHOULD only look under that name and MUST NOT fall back to bar.example.com or example.com.

SLP scopes are meant for one administrative domain and are likely meaningless to outsiders. So any remotely accessible service MUST be registered in the default scope (it MAY be in others too), and every DA advertised through DNS SRV MUST serve the default scope. Users searching a remote domain SHOULD search only the default scope. A UA uses DAs it has been configured with first, then DAs found via DNS SRV.

The RFC says this does not solve Internet-wide service discovery. An administrator may publish only some of the DAs through SRV, so local discovery MUST still use the standard SLP mechanisms, though an implementation MAY also use DNS SRV for local DAs in the default scope.
sections.eli5: Outsiders do not know your street's private room names, so the front hall, called the default scope, is the only place visitors are sent.

sections.title: Steps for Remote Discovery
sections.content:
To find services in remote domain D, a User Agent U does three things. It queries DNS for the _slpda SRV records of D, getting a list of remotely accessible DAs. It selects one DA from that list by priority and weight, as RFC 2782 describes. Then it queries that DA in the default scope for the desired services.

The RFC adds a caution: the services found this way are not necessarily remotely accessible.
sections.eli5: First look up who the helper is, then pick one, then ask that helper your question.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Supporting remote discovery exposes a domain's service information to the Internet. Standard SLP authentication SHOULD be used. An Internet-accessible DA SHOULD reject registrations and deregistrations it cannot authenticate, since otherwise any Service Agent could advertise any service. It SHOULD also authenticate queries outside the default scope. The security considerations of DNS SRV apply, and the DNS security extensions SHOULD be used for origin authentication and integrity protection of DNS data.
sections.eli5: If strangers can look up your helper, the helper should check who is asking and who is adding things to the list.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA registered the symbolic service name slpda for both tcp and udp, with this RFC as the reference. That is what makes the _slpda._tcp and _slpda._udp names usable.
sections.eli5: The special phone-book entry name was officially reserved so nobody else uses it for something different.
